noticias.contenido: Today, I’m talking with New York Governor Kathy Hochul, and I’ll just warn you — this episode moves really fast. It’s an election year, after all, with a shocking amount of tech policy at stake, and Governor Hochul has taken strong positions on almost every major tech issue there is. For example, Meta just reached a settlement with dozens of states, including New York, which will restrict how teens use platforms like Instagram in very specific ways. Governor Hochul is a strong supporter of those restrictions and more, as you’ll hear. But those come with a cost — widespread age verification means adults will also have to show ID to use the internet, which will essentially make it impossible to be anonymous online. Verge subscribers, don’t forget you get exclusive access to ad-free Decoder wherever you get your podcasts. Head here . Not a subscriber? You can sign up here . So I asked about that, and if these new restrictions amount to Meta conceding in a lawsuit that these kinds of regulations on speech might not pass First Amendment scrutiny if the governor were to try and impose them in a law. I had similar questions about New York’s restrictions on ghost guns, which prevent 3D printers from printing gun parts. That law is already being challenged — not in courts, but by activists like Cody Wilson, who runs the largest database of 3D-printable gun files and who has started altering those files in a process he calls “Hochulization” in order to show the ban is technically toothless. I asked the governor about this, and, well, you’ll hear her challenge Cody right back. Oh, but there’s more: We also talked about surveillance and Flock cameras, and, of course, the politics of AI and data centers in an election year. Governor Hochul signed a one-year moratorium on data center construction in July, and I wanted to know what she’s looking for when that expires to make data centers a workable proposition. We also talked a little about Mayor Zohran Mamdani in New York City and, of course, her org chart for the state government. This one is a lot, I think you’re going to like it. Okay: New York Governor Kathy Hochul, here we go. This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity. Governor Kathy Hochul, you are the governor of the state of New York! Welcome to Decoder . Thank you. Happy to be on. I have so much to talk to you about. We don’t have a ton of time, so we’re going to move fast. Are you up for it? I’m up. All right. I want to start with what I call the Decoder questions, lightning round style. I think the operation of your office and state government is really opaque to most people. So I ask everybody this question. How is the governor’s office structured? How did you make decisions about how to structure that office? How did you organize it? Governor at the top. Then there’s a leadership team, senior leadership team. There’s a secretary to the governor who is the top advisor. It sounds like the person taking notes at meetings, but the secretary of the governor is the most powerful non-elected position in the state. When I first became governor five years ago, I said, “I want the smartest, the best, the brightest people I could surround myself with.” I didn’t know a lot of these individuals, but they were highly recommended from having business experience, government experience, or technological experience. I said, “Bring me the smartest.” There’s a layer of senior team members. There’s one individual who oversees all the agencies. There are 45 different agencies for everything from the Department of Transportation to the environment to our housing development agency, economic development. It all trickles down to a pretty large bureaucracy. I’m the decision maker, but I take input from a lot of different levels of government before I make a final decision. But I’m a fairly quick decision-maker. Show me the facts and I can make a decision instantaneously. You took over in a complicated way from your predecessor and then you won reelection. Did you sit down and make an org chart of how you wanted your office to work? Yes, I did. How long did that take? I inherited one in a sense, but also early on I didn’t have a lot of tools. In fact, we had a hurricane in my first week. I didn’t know how to declare a disaster. I hadn’t hired that person yet, the head of emergency services. We were caught off-guard a little bit. The state still functioned, but I knew I needed to do more. I’m always in search of talent, smart people, and trying to rotate people in. Sometimes I start commissions like the Future Works Commission to bring in experts, not just from my administration but around the country, who understand the displacement of jobs because of AI: who’s most vulnerable, how we deal with that, and how we train people to be able to overcome those obstacles or to embrace AI as a possible career. I’m always finding ways to supplement my team with industry- or issue-specific experts. This question’s going to sound ridiculous, but I’ve asked a lot of people a variation of this question. Almost no one ever is going to sit down and say, “I need to write a new org chart for the governor’s office of New York.” Did you do that on a whiteboard? Did you open PowerPoint? Was it just you alone with a laptop? What was it actually like? Can I tell you something I’m embarrassed of, since you phrased it that way? I did it on a legal pad. Nice. Old school. Sorry. Yeah, pen and paper. No, it’s great. Very few people do that. You would be surprised at some of the answers we’ve gotten to questions like that. I just laid out, “This is what I need, this is the team I need.” Now that was five years ago. I’ve gotten a little better. I’d probably ask Claude or ChatGPT for some recommendations. Oh boy. We’re going to come to that. Don’t worry about it. You started answering this question, but this is the other Decoder question. How do you make decisions? What’s your framework? Bring in all the information as quickly as possible, pressure-test it, and then go with my gut. One of the more unique parts about structure in New York government is the relationship between the state and the city. We’re talking here in person in New York City. Mayor Zohran Mamdani has been pretty aggressive about going after billionaires and tech companies. Most recently the city went after Amazon for its labor practices. Do you think that’s been effective here? I need to make sure that New York City and the state overall continue to be a place where we support innovation, new jobs. Technology is leading the forefront right now. I’m really proud that we now have been named the number-one job creator for tech jobs in the country, surpassing California, which has always dominated in this space. That says something about our ecosystem and I want to foster that. I want people who have just an idea who can use technology to create something that no one else had ever conceived of and be successful in marketing it. That is what I’m leaning hard into. The mayor has his own approach, but I think overall we both want New York City to succeed. To me, success also means creating more opportunities for jobs because of the spinoff effect. Five guys in an office right in this building could lead to 500 jobs in a couple of years. Those opportunities help lift people out of their circumstances and achieve what I’m hoping for is more opportunity for more people. There’s a WeWork just above us. We got to go find those five guys. I’m asking specifically about the more aggressive approach the mayor has taken. He’s taken a very aggressive approach. And like you said, the numbers show that the billionaires didn’t run, they’re actually investing; the tech companies didn’t run, they’re actually hiring at a rate that surpasses San Francisco. Is that emboldening you to take a harsher regulatory approach to tech companies? I don’t just take a regulatory approach for the sake of doing it. I don’t raise taxes for the sake of doing it. I do things in a smart way when it’s necessary. For example, we have regulations on tech companies when it comes to social media for young people under the age of 18. My job is to protect the young people of our state because they have been spiraling with mental health challenges — exacerbated by the pandemic, yes, but many of them have not overcome that sense of doom and anxiety. It is pervasive in our teenagers particularly. I look at my role to regulate tech companies in that space. Before the Meta settlement, we had innovated and come up with probably three years’ worth of reforms to force the companies to do things that they are otherwise not doing on their own, and one would wish they would but that’s probably being too optimistic. We have in place, for example, no notifications to someone under the age of 18 between midnight and 6:00 AM. These kids need to sleep. We’re saying addictive algorithms can no longer bombard young people, having — this is a big deal — automatic privacy controls that are already set. Parents aren’t expected to understand every platform where their kids may go or any gaming site and have to get ahead of them. That it’s automatic using age verification is really important. Limiting access to AI chatbots for young people and making sure there are disclaimers so they understand this is not a real person that you think you’re having a relationship with: that’s an example where I think tech needs to be regulated. It went out of control and now the government has to perform a function to protect our residents and our young people, the most vulnerable. I don’t just regulate to stifle their growth. I want them to grow. It’s a smart, strategic, more surgical approach to regulations. I’m glad you brought up the Meta settlement. That’s obviously the big news this week. Meta settled with 47 states , including New York. I look at that settlement, I look at the list of controls that Meta has agreed to and my initial reaction was this is a bunch of stuff that, if passed as a law, would run into the teeth of the First Amendment. They are effectively speech restrictions, right? We’re going to prevent young people from using these platforms to speak at certain hours of the day. And maybe there’s some argument that overcomes the First Amendment objection, right? The teen health risk is so high that this is actually a narrowly crafted, strict scrutiny-abiding restriction, but we don’t know that. That actually hasn’t been challenged in court. Meta just gave that to you. Then there’s age verification to prove that you’re over 18. Even if you’re an adult, you still have to show the internet your ID, which is a big ask for people who are not covered by the restrictions. That’s a big swirl. Do you think you got concessions from Meta that you otherwise would not have been able to get if you just passed the law? No, we actually have laws in New York that are more restrictive than some of what Meta has agreed to. Are you worried about the First Amendment implications of some of those laws? No, I’m not. And here’s why: we have an opportunity and the responsibility to protect our residents. The First Amendment is when the government says that we’re limiting your speech. Not having notifications that keep you awake all night when you’re a 13-year-old is not restricting your First Amendment right to free speech. There is a difference. Sometimes the First Amendment is used as any kind of government regulation. People will say, “Oh my God, you’re violating the First Amendment” or any of the other amendments. I’m an attorney. I look at it closely. I don’t do things to violate amendments or any laws. It’s not my practice. We’re smart about how we structure these and make sure that we’re protecting First Amendment rights as well as protecting young people from having their mental health monetized by companies who have a profit motive. It’s almost like cigarette smoking. The earlier you get them, the longer you’re going to keep them hooked. Young people should not be bombarded with the addictive algorithms or be subjected to the bullying that goes on. Someone who’s thinking about suicide searches for “suicide” and is now told different ways to commit suicide. That is terrifying for parents. Parents actually appreciate the fact that they have a voice in government. Maybe it’s because I’m the first mom governor in New York that I understand this. I’ve raised kids. I know the pressures they’re under. Something else we did: I’m really proud of the fact that we’re the biggest state in the nation to have come up with a full ban on cell phones in schools. Now you can say it’s violating their First Amendment rights. I’m saying I’m protecting them from a lifetime of addiction to a device where they no longer have human relationships. You asked how I make decisions. Sometimes I go with my gut, sometimes I want confirmation from the real world and I go out there and talk to people in schools and in cafeterias and have a lot of conversations with young people. When I did round tables around the state of New York for about a solid year to get information, [students] were so anxious about missing a notification. “The girls are meeting in the restroom to plan activities for Friday night and I just got excluded and I’m also getting knocked out because of what I’m wearing. And now they’ve got a picture of me in an inappropriate way being sent around the school.” These kids are paralyzed. One young person, probably a sixth grader, said to me, “You’ve got to save us from ourselves. We can’t put these down. We’ll be ostracized.” That’s when I took it to heart and I said, “I will protect you. I’ll protect these kids.” We literally instituted this in September. The survey results from just this past May show anywhere from 75% to 80% of the schools surveyed have been overwhelmingly positive. The kids who resisted at first are now making friends in person. There’s more communication. They’re learning the interpersonal skills that you’d want your future workforce to have, and they’re playing games at lunchtime. They’re playing cards. They have baseball cards they’re trading. They’re playing chess, bingo. It’s almost silly, but they’re just being kids again. And so they’ve got plenty of time for the stresses of the real world. They can become hooked on social media later on in life. They can get hooked on their device. They can do all this later, but why do we rob their childhood from them? Sure. I’ve got kids in New York public schools. I’m reasonably happy about the bans. I’m not excited about my daughter ever getting a phone. But if you were to do this straightforwardly in a legislative way, particularly the restrictions that Meta has agreed to, you would have to build out some record and you would have to do some balance of harms analysis. Here, Meta agreeing to age verification means that I, an adult, have to tell them how old I am with some tool, probably by showing them my ID. That is a big burden on me, an adult, that has nothing to do with the safety of the kids. That to me feels like it might not pass the scrutiny that the courts would provide if Meta was like, “Actually, this is too much of a burden.” How do you address that? Because the big concern here is that you’ve actually, instead of saying age verification for teens, de-anonymized the internet. The proof is the fact that Meta agreed to this in a settlement. Meta’s looking out for its corporate interest. I’m looking out for my interests as a citizen. Meta’s looking out for its ability to get more citizens like you to be engaged with it so it can make more money off of you and sell you more products. It’s in Meta’s interest to have you engage. The fact that they’re willing to step back— Right. They don’t care if I have to de-anonymize myself to look at Instagram ads for things I don’t need to buy. I’m saying I would like to be anonymous on the internet and if we put age verification everywhere, which is one of the consequences of this agreement, that every platform is going to have to start doing age verification at scale. I won’t be able to use the internet without constantly identifying myself to prove my age. I’m sure there’s a path forward that doesn’t require you to do this constantly. I’m not aware that you’d have to do it every single time you participate, every time you go to a site. I’m not aware that you’d have to do it that way. Let me find that out. I’m not going to say something without knowing that answer, but it’s an interesting point you raise. It really is. But I’m focused on the fact that we did gather data around the country to find out what is happening to our young people today. I cannot rely on parents to know how to stop this from happening, because the parents are the ones telling me, “Please do something. I don’t know how to stop this. My kid is spiraling.” One mom told me that she has her husband leave work every day at three to make sure their son, who’s being bullied in school and harassed and going to dark sites, doesn’t commit suicide when he goes home. Who wants to live with that specter? That was not the case when I was a kid, or my kids were kids. The world has changed and again, it is not a no to progress or innovation. I have thousands of examples of me inviting tech companies here. Even Micron, the largest private-sector investment in American history. 50,000 jobs are happening up in Syracuse because I went after them aggressively. They’ll be open in two years. This is extraordinary, building the memory chips that are necessary to power AI in New York state. My credentials are impeccable when it comes to inviting innovation in, but when there are areas where we need guardrails to protect individuals, I’m going to step in and do this. I feel good about this. This is a decision that we’ve made and I think it’s overwhelmingly supported by many parents. Young people someday will appreciate the fact that they were spared from this, and other people who adapt to this, this is the way it is. So much tech regulation, particularly for the last decade, has run into the First Amendment. Again, my view of it is we’ve avoided the First Amendment conversation by talking about Section 230 or other red herrings that allow us to not talk about the fact that a lot of this looks like speech regulation and expression regulation in important ways. Another good example of this, which I think will be developed, is the restriction on ghost guns in New York state. The idea is that you should not be able to 3D-print gun parts in New York state. We have a story just this week about Cody Wilson , who printed the first 3D-printed gun. He’s put out a tool to defeat the way that the law is designed to work. He calls it “Hochulization,” where he’s going to de-fingerprint the hashes of 3D-printed gun files so that whatever tool is scanning at the 3D printer level will not see that it’s a gun and print it anyway. That’s a cat and mouse game. That is a technological arms race. You can tell Cody I will get ahead of him next. I can’t always be on the forefront when I see someone intentionally thwarting a law. It is the law that you cannot have 3D-printed guns in the state of New York. And if you think it’s okay to have someone in their kitchen who may have severe mental health problems who wants to shoot up kids in your school, make a ghost gun at their kitchen table or create a munitions factory where there was none, with no regulations, no background checks, no nothing, and people broadcast that as if it’s a proper thing to do is challenge me on that, then I say go for it. Because you’re trampling in the wrong space. The question I’m asking is about implementation. I understand the desire to prevent guns from being 3D-printed and I understand that probably a lot of people would prefer that not happen. Yeah, it’s bad. It sucks. It’s wrong. But implementing that means at some point the printer itself has to know “this thing is a gun and I’m not allowed to do this.” That’s right. That is a kind of regulation on expression. We have a case for an open source e-reader that looks like a gun that people have made just to see if it will trip the software detector. Even though it’s not a gun, it looks like a gun, and there’s some line in there that is very complicated for a government regulation to address. How do you view that? Do you want the printers to literally look at things that look like guns or do you want it to be more technical, more like a database or a registry? I want to make sure that we’re getting the objective I’m looking for and I’ll figure it out. As I said, I assemble the smartest people when I make decisions, especially in the area of technology where the typical government employee is not proficient. So I’m going to use the foundation I have, but then go out there and say, “Tell me how to make sure that no one can thwart what I’m trying to do here,” and I’ll get it done. If we miss the first time, I’ll do it the second time and I’ll do it the third time because I’m not going to allow this to happen. Yes, there are other restrictions that occur. I get that. It’s not ideal, but I also didn’t think it was a smart idea for people to manufacture weapons of mass destruction at their kitchen table and kill kids. So I’m going to be the one who says no. I’d rather have the regulation that protects and prevents it. Use 3D printers for any kind of good. You can make all kinds of things with 3D printers. It’s not a ban on 3D printing. It is a use that is illegal because you cannot have a gun in the state of New York without having had a background check, having regulation, having it registered. We have all kinds of rules, which is one of the reasons why we are one of the safest states in America. Lowest gun homicide deaths in America. It’s extraordinary, because the rules are working. So not everyone loves rules. I get it. This is not the wild west. This is New York. We’re going to do it right. If there’s a theme emerging in this conversation, it’s how much can the government watch what happens on my computer and how much can it tell me what I can do with my computer? Which is maybe a 40-year-old conversation, but it’s more and more relevant over time. We’re saying we’re going to restrict how teenagers can use their phones. We’re going to restrict what you can print on a 3D printer. The flip side of that is… I would say the backlash to surveillance is bipartisan. The backlash to Flock cameras is deeply bipartisan. It’s scrambling party lines. Right. You’ve allocated budget for police departments to modernize, to install Flock cameras. How are you viewing that backlash to surveillance? I understand the anxiety around this. I truly do. But you see how it’s all the same, right? I do not have complete regulation over someone’s use of their computer. That’s an overstatement. It just is. We have a very narrow, specific purpose and a government objective to protect young people, because the companies have gone too far. If they had put these controls in place themselves, when the data was starting to show them that this is harmful to kids, [but they didn’t]. They stopped letting their own kids use this, but let everybody else be subjected to this, knowing the harms. That’s when the government has to step in and regulate business. We don’t do it as a first position. My view is more hands off. Innovate, do good things, sell your product. Great. This is called capitalism in America. A 3D printer, those are great. Until I find out they’re making guns that can kill people from them or be able to convert a Glock. Maybe it’s a legal Glock that you have registered to you, that’s great, but you can get this little piece of plastic that’s the size of a Lego and insert that and all of a sudden it can fire countless rounds per minute. Now it’s a weapon of mass destruction. The government has to be watching to an extent. Watch for excesses, but not to stifle personal use, not to stifle innovation, not to stifle the companies. When they go too far or they don’t self-regulate, using data that they have internally and ignoring it, thinking they can get away with it, that’s where we are today. I’m just connecting the dots between “I want to use my printer in some way,” “there’s a connection to the government that says yes or no,” and how people feel about technology like Flock — “I want to drive my car too fast on the highway and an automated license plate reader is going to track that and send me a ticket in the mail.” Or “cops are going to use this in ways, good and bad, and sometimes they’re going to go over the line and there’s not enough regulation,” or “I don’t want these cameras at all.” Which is what we hear from so many people in so many communities, across party lines. Actually let me read you a quote — To the extent that they’re being abused, that has to stop. Sure. The CEO of Flock recently said to a lot of people, including The Verge , that he was wrong to assume that the regulatory process would provide protections for civil liberties. He assumed that state and local governments would provide controls for Flock to prevent things like cops over-searching the database or tracking people. Tracking a lot of ex-girlfriends, for example, is a thing that we hear about cops using Flock for. That’s a pretty stunning indictment. The state is rolling out cameras to track people without the necessary controls, and the company providing the camera is saying, “Well actually you were wrong about this.” The state is not rolling these out. I give money for all kinds of technology. The localities are the ones that decide how they want that spent. I do not have a contract with Flock. That is a mischaracterization. But the money provided does not come with controls? I use the money for overtime for police. Computers in police vehicles is primarily the main focus of this. And to the extent that there are license plate readers, that’s different from the Flock cameras which are automatically transmitting information without human intervention, which is what I object to. Okay. If there’s a police officer that says, “This person is wanted for murder, let’s go get them,” you’d be happy if we went after them. But this is not just to have AI or a machine make an automatic referral of information to other agencies, whether it’s ICE or anybody else. That’s not what we’re talking about here in the state of New York. That’s not what we want to happen. If I need to tighten up regulations in that space, I will. I have no trouble looking— Can you connect that to the money that you’re allocating for this technology and say, “You have to use it this way?” Yes, we can. We can look at it. That’s an observation. That’s new information to me, that we should be having restrictions on and how they’re using it. Absolutely. What would you ask of the CEO of Flock in order to make that job easier? I’d tell him to make sure that the information can only be amassed a certain way. It has to be reviewed with human eyes to make a decision on whether or not this has to be forwarded to another law enforcement agency, the FBI or someone’s wanted list. That’s basically the purpose we want it for. I don’t want Big Brother. I don’t want unfettered surveillance of Americans that makes them anxious. It goes against the sense of liberty that we all have and deserve to have living in this country. This is not a country where the government should be monitoring everything you do, but to the extent that we have to stop crime and thwart the criminals who are always trying to take steps ahead of us, I have to get ahead of that as well, and try to manage that or else we have a lawless society. People are getting harmed and then it’s a failure of government to intercede. We’ll come to data centers, but I think data centers are doing this as well. There is some kind of realignment happening. These are not right- or left-coded issues. They’re not Democratic or Republican issues. They are scrambling that traditional very, very strong party ties that have existed for almost a decade in this country. Surveillance is one, data centers are another. Do you see that — that there’s a scrambling here? There’s nothing wrong with that. I welcome that. I have been waiting a long time for there to be more issues that people, all Americans, can galvanize behind and find some commonality. When I’m doing roundtables around the state, and I’ve done many, I don’t know if I’m talking to Democrats or Republicans. All I know is these are people worried about what’s happening in their communities with hyperscale data centers being built, making noise, causing disruption, and consuming energy. Is that driving up their own utility bills? They’re anxious about this. No, this is important. It’s an important time in our history to find that there are common interests and maybe that’s a breakthrough if you can have elected officials remind people like that: “Listen, you’re agreeing with your Republican neighbor and you’re a Democrat or vice versa.” That’s good. Greg Abbott, the governor of Texas, followed our leadership on the moratorium on hyperscale data centers — not the smaller ones for university research or educational institutions or healthcare institutions. We are very specific and these are the large-scale data centers. But to have the state of Texas follow our lead, that says something. That says something — that Americans overall are saying enough is enough. The rudest version of this question is: Doesn’t that just say that it’s an election year? No. You don’t think so? No. This only became an issue fairly recently in the state of New York. We were recently bombarded with 30 applications. That was the aha moment for me to say, “Wait a minute, if we powered all of these requests for approvals, how much power would I have left for everybody else in the state?” I’ll give one example: in upstate New York, there’s a county, St. Lawrence County. Five applications for data centers are pending right now. I said, “How much power would all those consume?” The equivalent of everything I would generate with one nuclear reactor. So I’m trying to build more nuclear power. I want to get ahead of the game and try to reduce the cost of power, make sure we never have shortages. All the work to get one nuclear reactor would be consumed by five data centers in one of my 62 counties. You expect your government to say, “Wait a minute.” If this had come up to me five years ago, I would have done it five years ago. This has nothing to do with electoral politics at all. In fact, my opponent embraces data centers. The President embraces data centers. They’re the ones on the wrong side of history on this one. If they were smart, they’d say, “You know what, the governor’s right. Let’s just stand out on this issue because our constituents are not with us on this.” This is what I mean by a realignment issue. The President does embrace the data centers. He calls them, “Money printing machines,” which I think is very funny. Unclear if he knows what actually happens at a data center. But then you have, right in Texas, a similar moratorium. We just ran a story about Republican voters in Florida , hardcore MAGA voters, people who organized the Stop the Steal rally saying they would not vote for Byron Donalds if he won the primary. He won the primary, he’s going to run on data centers. We’ll see if he adjusts his position, but that’s a realignment. And I’m wondering if the answer is just in a year’s time when your moratorium expires, it’ll be over and we’ll start building again, or if there’s something specific you’re looking for as a solution to bring construction back online. A couple of points. In one year from now, the communities in the state of New York that want to host hyperscale data centers will have far more tools at their disposal than they do today, which is what I’m trying to give them. I want them to have what I call my community investments framework. I have studied what data centers have done for communities all over America. I have a list. I know that in South Bend, Indiana, the community received $143 million of benefits. Other areas have had bonuses for teachers and supporting roads and infrastructure, energy infrastructure. I want our residents to know that their local elected officials have gotten the best deal they possibly can because right now, think about the negotiation that goes on between a small-town, maybe a part-time mayor, a small economic development staff, and they’re supposed to negotiate against a tech giant. It’s not going well. I want to help them out. Why are there tax breaks in the state of New York for a data center? They have more money than God. They don’t need tax breaks that hurt my small farmers and my small towns. This is where they’re going. They’re not coming to New York City. These are going to rural areas, generally Republican areas, which is very interesting. But also the water consumption. Are they all using the hyperloop? Are they doing something else? Do they need to make the noise they do? Do they need to be this size? I’ve asked these questions. In fact, I posed a challenge to the data companies: “You’ve created a powerful force that is changing civilization as we know it, the way we communicate, the way we work, the way we live with AI. Why don’t you ask AI how to create power that uses less energy, uses less space? Can you go vertical? Maybe you can go vertical, take up less farmland, less space, but it costs more. Well, then pay more.” They’re trying to go vertical. They’re trying to go all the way up to space. [Laughs] Maybe the whole thing should go up to space. That’s the other question. We are talking about one that’s seven miles large. Seven miles, I can’t even conceive of that. We have some already that I’ve looked at in the East Coast and they’re huge. What happens when the technology changes and they do this underwater or in space or they figure out a way to make it much smaller? Nuclear reactors can now be small modular reactors. Things change and what happens to the community when they’re left with this monstrosity left behind? You have to be thinking about this in advance. I told the people who work at the big AI labs that I was talking to you and I said, “What do you want to know?” Now I will concede they all think AI is a net good. They all think it’s going to be great. We have some people in our audience who do not agree with them, but speaking for them, they all think AI will be a net good. It will improve humanity. The question was, “What do you want the hyperscalers to give?” If you believe that AI progress will be a net good and inevitable, what is the ask that enables that development to happen? I will restate my challenge. I understand you need the power. I have harnessed AI in the state of New York, in state government in a way no other governor has. I have used AI to look at every single rule, regulation, policy, board, and commission. Has that been effective? Is that just you alone with Claude? How does that work? I don’t do it myself. [Laughs] I have smarter people than me that do. All right. Fair enough. Literally I said, “What would it take for us to look at every rule in the books? And are they smart? Are they obsolete? Are they too expensive? Are they too burdensome?” Let’s ask those questions. I like to rethink. I’m always challenging the status quo. It’s how I’m hardwired. Let’s look at the state government. People think it’s intractable. I say we can make it leaner, smarter, more efficient. And in literally a month, I had a list of thousands of recommendations, what would have taken five to 10 years for humans to do. I announced the first 50 already: we saved over a million and a half hours for New York businesses and individuals when it comes to filling out redundant forms. My first 50 out of thousands, saving millions of dollars in other areas. There was a $25 fee to take your dog hunting with you. You had to pay for a $25,000 bond to move a mobile home on a highway. Why? Get rid of that. Why does someone have to do that? A woman could not work after midnight if she was pregnant. You had to have special permission to do that. Sending information by telegraph and telegram. I just looked at this and said, “I used AI as a force of good to rethink state government.” So I’m not opposed, but I’m saying to them, “You already know what a next-generation data center looks like. It does not have to be this big. It does not have to use this much power. Figure it out now before there’s even more hostility towards you. Your public relations are dreadful by the way. No one understands what you’re trying to do and you come in like big bullies and you think you can run all over a little community, maybe you did in the early years.” They’re getting a little smarter now. They’re starting to give more community benefits, but they’ll figure it out. Let me ask you about this. You’re a politician in a campaign year. I hear so much from the AI labs that what they have is a marketing problem, that if people could only understand the benefits, if they communicated them more broadly, they would win far more hearts and minds and people would be all behind this build out. I personally disagree with that. Everybody sees AI overviews in Google all day long. A billion people have used ChatGPT. The products are known to people and the capabilities are known to people. Maybe there’s some set of very advanced capabilities like the things you’ve described you’ve done in government that would unlock even more. But I don’t think they have a marketing problem. They have an attitude problem. To some extent they have a product problem. I don’t think the products are good enough to support the asks, and these are enormous asks as you’ve been describing. How would you handle that for them? How would you say, “Look, these are big build outs, the potential benefits to humanity are high and from the government side, here’s what you actually need to say and promise to people in order to work on this productively”? It’s not that. People know the benefits. Your kid gets a bite, you’re going to take a picture and ask Claude, “Is this a tick bite or a mosquito bite? Do I need to worry about this?” The way that medicine has even been integrated into people’s lives, asking questions. It’s already being employed in a positive way for the people who want to use it in a positive way, as you’ve said. The data centers, the hyperscalers, have become the physical manifestation of people’s anxiety about the future. Think about all the young people that I literally spent years myself telling, “Go into STEM careers, kids, learn science and math. You’ll have a job forever. Oh yes, study coding and computer science. The jobs are going to be there.” Guess what? Those are the jobs that are going first. People are anxious about displacement. They’re worried. They’re not opposed to advancement and technology in the future, but where do they fit into it? Government has to be addressing that anxiety. When people see the data centers, they’re thinking, “Oh geez, that’s my job that could be gone.” [AI labs] have to do a better job addressing the concerns that people have. Don’t make a big show about laying off 10,000 people in your company and literally tell them it’s because of AI. I had people who were displaced sitting in my office. They’re told they’re gone because of AI. That was more of a shareholders’ play to show your shareholders you’re streamlining and saving money, but that’s a lot of people’s lives you just ruined. That’s what’s going on. Those are the conversations that I’m hearing in places where they’ll never see a data center, like here in New York City. Their challenge is to help people see that this is not [negative]. If they can’t prove this proposition, then they’re probably going to lose the battle for the hearts and minds. But show us the jobs that can be created. What other jobs should people be going to? When I’m told that, “81% of the jobs likely to be displaced are held by women” — Women took this long to finally make it into the workplace and in significant positions or positions where it’s administrative or legal secretaries or legal assistants, even new lawyers. All the jobs that you can think of are held by women. A woman might be the primary breadwinner. If she thinks her job’s going to be gone because of AI, she’s not going to love an AI company. She’s going to say, “Wait a minute, what about me?” They need to figure out what the AI future looks like. Tell us right now the skills that are required. What should I be teaching in schools? What should we say the state education department should be teaching? What courses should students be taking in college to prepare the next generation of workers, so they will not be in that displacement? We have a whole lot of people who are already in that vulnerable spot. The individuals just getting out of college, those who are mid-career, what are they supposed to do? I saw this personally. I’m from Buffalo. Buffalo Bills fan. I’ll put that right out here now. We haven’t talked about the stadium , but we can get there. We’ll get to the stadium. We saved the Bills. That’s all you need to know. They’re not in another state. There you go. They are the Buffalo Bills, and they weren’t going to be. But not far from there, my parents used to live in a trailer park near the steel mill. Everybody worked at the steel plant, Bethlehem Steel. It was the best job you could get. My dad worked there, my grandpa worked there, my uncles worked there. In 1982, they picked up and left town. No one thought about the workers, the 20,000 workers in my town that now just lost their livelihoods. They left. My point is that I lived through that. I will not let that happen now. That’s what people are anxious about, losing their livelihoods. I just want to connect two dots here right at the end, because I’m really happy you brought up the idea that it’s the physical manifestation of anxiety. This is a trope, I think, in the tech industry. It’s true: data centers are big, they’re noisy. You can look at them and you can say stop. But we started out talking about all the things you might want to keep people from doing on computers, or keep computers from doing to people, maybe more importantly. Again, it’s been a decade of attempts to do this. We don’t have a privacy law in this country. There are all these things that we don’t have because of the First Amendment. We were unable to overcome the First Amendment to regulate social media in some very big, important ways. You can stop a data center. The power of NIMBYism is strong in America, and the tools exist to stop it. Is this the wrong tool for the job to say we’re going to do land use and NIMBYism instead of regulating labor and employment and the future of young people more directly? There are two different dynamics here, a big difference. One is the application of AI and how it’s being utilized. I’m asking about the mechanism. I understand the goals, but it’s the mechanism that I’m really thinking about here. The mechanism of the data centers, of the power they’re creating? We might want to regulate AI to make sure there are more and better jobs, or protect women in the workplace. The mechanism that we’re using to get to that outcome is we’re going to stop the data centers until they make better promises. See, I don’t see it as one or the other. Both are occurring right now. But stopping the data centers is not my objective here. It is to make sure that they do it right for the communities that want it. There’s a big difference. Maybe the companies will negotiate in a way, or they might say, “I guess we didn’t need that much space,” or “Yeah, we figured out a way to make it not noisy at all. You won’t even know we’re there,” or “We’re going to do a better job shielding this.” Everyone talks about Loudoun County, Virginia… We have a big story about Loudoun County coming next week. You know why I know Loudoun County? Because when I said my family had to leave Buffalo because there were no jobs, guess where they went to? I’m one of six kids; four of my siblings landed in Loudoun County many years ago when it was all farmland. Now they have in the backyard of their homes these massive data centers. For a while it was like, “Wow, look at this. Our taxes can go down. We’re benefiting from this.” But do you know what? After a while, the tax abatement stopped, or the benefits stopped over a length of time. Now they’re starting to see their utility bills and property taxes go up. What they were sold years ago when they were the test case of a community that had lots of data centers, believe me, there’s buyer’s remorse. Not just for my siblings, but for many people who are saying, “You know what? We didn’t get the best deal after all. What are we doing here?” I learned from other examples around the state, around the country, around the world, and I want to make sure that what we do in New York is based on the soundest, smartest practices. We embrace AI. Do there have to be data centers? If they have to be there, are they doing it in the best way? I’m going to challenge them.I know I’m going to keep pushing them to do better. When I first became an elected official in my small town, that’s when all the tech comms came and they all wanted their own cell tower. “Everybody’s going to want their own cell phone. We have to have our own freestanding tower.” I said, “Those are ugly. I don’t want these giant cell towers in neighborhoods and everywhere. They’re horrific.” So I said to them, “Why don’t you co-locate? Can’t you all go on one tower, you and your five competitors?” “No, that’s not possible.” “Okay. Can you go on top of a water tower? Can you go on top of a tall building?” “No, no, no. We have to…” So I passed the toughest law regulating cell towers in the entire state in my small town, and I forced them to pay me for the ability. I said, “I’m going to challenge you. I’m going to get outside experts when you tell me you can’t do something, and you’re going to pay for the cost of that consultant.” They did. Guess what? They co-locate. They’re on top of water towers. My town does not have cell towers everywhere, but we were told it had to be that way because I presume it was the cheapest, the best for them, the easiest for them to just throw these up. I said, “What happens when the technology changes and you’re bouncing this off of satellites?” This was a long time ago. I said, “I don’t want to be looking at any kind of towers here.” I made them put in a bond. They had to pay money for us to be able to dismantle this and take it down, even if it’s 50 years from now. I know how to do this. I’ve done it before. And that’s what I’m trying to do for New York: use my experiences on how to manage this. We didn’t say no to cell phones. We said yes to cell phones. We say yes to AI, but in a way that the companies have to be challenged by the government to do it better because their own profit motives will let them do whatever’s cheapest and fastest for them. That’s not necessarily serving the public good. That’s what I have to protect. Governor, you’ve given us a ton of time. You’ve answered a lot of questions here. We did go fast. It’s an election year. I am very curious about this big realignment scramble. Give people your view of what to expect in this election year as surveillance, data centers, and AI scramble our traditional party lines. How do you think that’s going to play out? What is top of mind is very much the data centers nationally, and it’s fascinating to me to see that in races for Congress and governor in other states, they’re using this as a political point. I could not have foreseen that six months ago. Public opinion has shifted so quickly. But again, regardless of what happens in the election, I do think Democrats will prevail for many, many reasons. There’s so much going on, and we can get to other topics on trade wars with Canada and how it’s having an effect. You brought up the Bills. I want to talk about the NFL’s antitrust exemption. But that’s for another time. [Laughs] Can we just talk about the fact that the Buffalo Bills stayed in Buffalo? I fought hard. Look, I’m a Packers fan. What do you think the Bears should do? We got another hour on that. I actually like small-town markets. I like the Packers. I used to follow them closely. Way before you were born, I was a big AFC fan. The Bills used to play the Packers all the time. So we can talk sports anytime. But I just want to leave people with this sense. I believe that Democrats will take back the House and the Senate and position themselves to take back the White House, but we have to do it in a smart way that shows that we are attuned to the anxieties of Americans. I know that people are very anxious about their future, their jobs, how they’re going to take care of their families in a world where AI seems to be so ever-present, and it is that data center that scares them. We can do more to shape that, make sure that people understand that’s in one sense a necessary evil, but that evil doesn’t have to be as evil as it is. Make it less evil, and people will adapt and adjust and understand this. The companies are complicit in this sense of, “We can do what we want because we’re so big.” Americans, when they go to vote, want people who are going to stand up and not just roll over. They have a president and Republicans in Congress, my Republican opponent, who are rolling over trying to convince people that, “No, this is good,” when in fact you have people like me and some others who are saying, “Let’s do this smart. Let’s be thoughtful about this. I’m not going to roll over. I don’t roll over for anybody.” That’s the impact on the elections. Democrats are going to win. Governor, thank you so much for your time. Thank you for implying that I’m young. That was very nice of you. I really appreciate it. [Laughs] It’s all relative, right? Questions or comments? Hit us up at decoder@theverge.com. We really do read every email!

noticias.titulo: El plan Trump para dar al Pentágono participación en las riquezas petroleras de Venezuela: 'WSJ'
noticias.resumen: El acuerdo petrolero entre Venezuela y Estados Unidos tiene varias zonas grises. 'The Wall Street Journal' señala que el pacto transforma al Gobierno estadounidense de intermediario a inversor en sí mismo, lo que realizaría a través del Pentágono. Entretanto, 'The New York Times' describe el historial de investigaciones en Suiza y España contra Alejandro Betancourt, el empresario venezolano detrás del acuerdo. Fue su historial operativo con el crudo el que definió su selección como clave en este acuerdo.

noticias.titulo: ChatGPT and Reddit now face EU's toughest online safety rules
noticias.resumen: Explosive growth comes with a new regulatory burden in the European Union.
noticias.contenido: OpenAI’s ChatGPT will have to comply with tougher EU rules such as removing illegal content or face potential fines, the European Commission said on Monday, as Brussels grapples with how its existing digital regulation applies to rapidly evolving AI services. The Commission said the chatbot, social media forum Reddit, and gaming platform Roblox would be classified as so-called very large online platforms under the EU Digital Services Act, its landmark online safety regime. The designation means all three services will face additional obligations such as removing illegal content and protecting the privacy and security of minors and could face fines of up to 6 percent of their global revenue if they fail to comply. noticias.resumen: If you sit in an Australian park or garden for long enough, chances are you might catch a flash of brilliant feathers out of the corner of your eye: the superb fairywren. With its bright blue and soft brown plumage, it was voted Australia’s “bird of the year” in 2021, “narrowly defeating the tawny frogmouth […]
noticias.contenido: If you sit in an Australian park or garden for long enough, chances are you might catch a flash of brilliant feathers out of the corner of your eye: the superb fairywren. With its bright blue and soft brown plumage, it was voted Australia’s “bird of the year” in 2021, “narrowly defeating the tawny frogmouth in a nail-biting finish” in a poll by Guardian Australia and BirdLife Australia. Yet, despite its seeming abundance in gardens and backyards, this iconic bird is showing worrying signs of decline. Superb fairywrens (Malurus cyaneus) are found in any habitat with dense shrubbery along the east coast of Australia, parts of South Australia and Tasmania. Despite being categorized as least concern on the IUCN Red List, a long-term study of superb fairywrens conducted in the Australian National Botanic Gardens in Canberra determined that they’re disappearing, with climate change impacting their survival. Scientists have been monitoring these superb fairywrens since 1988, and research led by the Australian National University’s Cockburn Group found that this population has rapidly declined. In a recently published article in Nature Communications, the researchers write that this “common species … is in imminent danger, with virtually no time or way to prevent it.” Female superb fairywrens have a soft brown plumage unlike their bright blue male counterparts. noticias.contenido: In 2015, the remote coastal fjords of southern Patagonia turned into a whale graveyard. That June, scientists found 337 dead and decomposing sei whales, a species of baleen whale, on the beaches between the Gulf of Penas and Puerto Natales in Chile. Researchers flew over the area, then took samples from the rotting bodies, trying to find clues as to why this happened. It was later reported to be the largest mass baleen whale mortality event on record. Data collected to determine the cause proved inconclusive, however. Scientists thought the most likely explanation was a toxic red tide provoked by pollution, a strong El Niño event and climate change. What researchers now know for certain, after using very high-resolution satellite images, is that the stranding occurred at least two months before the whales were found. “It’s quite shocking, really,” Penny Clarke, a whale scientist at the British Antarctic Survey (BAS), told Mongabay in a video call. “Think that these whales are about the size of a bus, and there’s 300 … of them, and nobody knew about it for about two months.” The massive stranding in Chile had one bright spot: It offered an important opportunity to test the use of satellite technology to monitor strandings and support data collection on whale mortality. More than 10 years later, Clarke and her BAS colleagues not only use satellite imagery to identify different whale species by observing flippers and flukes in the water, but can spot whale strandings almost anywhere in the…This article was originally published on Mongabay

noticias.resumen: Mun Jong-gi llegó a Japón desde Corea del Sur con una autorización para permanecer apenas 15 días. Según la policía japonesa, había utilizado el pasaporte de su hermano menor y buscaba algo bastante concreto: empleos mejor pagados que los que podía conseguir en su país. El hombre no regresó cuando venció el permiso. De hecho, 33 años después, una información recibida por la policía descubrió hasta dónde habían llegado aquellos 15 días. De 15 días a 33 años. noticias.contenido: Mun Jong-gi llegó a Japón desde Corea del Sur con una autorización para permanecer apenas 15 días. Según la policía japonesa, había utilizado el pasaporte de su hermano menor y buscaba algo bastante concreto: empleos mejor pagados que los que podía conseguir en su país. El hombre no regresó cuando venció el permiso. De hecho, 33 años después, una información recibida por la policía descubrió hasta dónde habían llegado aquellos 15 días. De 15 días a 33 años. Mun Jong-gi tenía 39 años cuando llegó a Japón en septiembre de 1993 y recibió permiso para permanecer en el país durante únicamente 15 días . La policía. como decíamos, sostiene que entró utilizando el pasaporte de su hermano menor y que su intención era encontrar trabajos que le permitieran ganar más dinero que en Corea del Sur. Ocurre que cuando terminó aquel plazo no regresó: al contrario, permaneció en Japón y, según las investigaciones , continuó viviendo allí prácticamente de manera ininterrumpida hasta 2026. En Xataka Japón ha encontrado los tres problemas más graves de la llegada masiva de turistas. Y ninguno tiene que ver con los turistas No es solo cuánto tiempo, sino cómo lo hizo. Durante esas más de tres décadas, Mun habría sobrevivido realizando trabajos por días y otros empleos ocasionales, aunque las informaciones disponibles no explican quién lo contrataba ni cómo resolvió durante tanto tiempo otros aspectos cotidianos que normalmente requieren documentación en la nación nipona. Tampoco existe por ahora una explicación completa de cómo consiguió permanecer tantos años sin que su situación migratoria desembocara antes en una detención. Lo que sí sabemos es que no fue una investigación iniciada en los años noventa la que finalmente permitió encontrarlo: su caso apareció ante la policía más de tres décadas después de su llegada. La pista. La secuencia que acabó con su vida clandestina comenzó en junio de 2026, cuando la policía recibió información sobre una persona que presuntamente residía ilegalmente en Japón. La Policía de la Prefectura de Shizuoka abrió entonces una investigación que terminó conduciendo hasta Mun en Yaizu, una ciudad costera situada al suroeste de Tokio. Finalmente fue detenido el pasado 26 de agosto de 2026, con 72 años. Durante el interrogatorio habría reconocido las acusaciones y explicado que había ido encadenando trabajos ocasionales durante su estancia. La paradoja. La diferencia se debe a una peculiaridad jurídica importante para entender el caso. Aunque su autorización de 15 días expiró en 1993, las informaciones japonesas señalan que la permanencia irregular pasó a ser específicamente castigada penalmente tras un cambio legislativo que entró en vigor en febrero de 2000 . Por eso la policía sitúa el periodo objeto de la acusación desde ese momento: Mun habría permanecido irregularmente en Japón durante casi 33 años, pero la infracción penal que sustenta su arresto comprende aproximadamente los últimos 26. 300.000 casos similares. Mun desembarcó además en un Japón muy diferente al actual en materia migratoria. En 1993, precisamente el año de su llegada, el país contabilizaba 298.646 extranjeros que habían superado el periodo de estancia autorizado, una cifra récord y más de cuatro veces superior a la actual. En enero de 2026 quedaban registrados 68.488 , de modo que su historia comenzó en el momento de máxima expansión del fenómeno y terminó cuando Japón había conseguido reducirlo drásticamente. La búsqueda de un mejor sueldo. La motivación que Mun habría explicado a los investigadores resulta mucho más convencional y simple que la extraordinaria duración de su estancia: el hombre había viajado a Japón porque esperaba ganar más dinero trabajando allí. Lo excepcional es que aquella decisión temporal tomada a finales de 1993 acabara prolongándose durante aproximadamente 12.000 días , hasta convertir una autorización de dos semanas en prácticamente media vida. Tenía unos 39 años cuando entró y 72 cuando la policía llamó finalmente a su puerta. En Xataka Los pasaportes más y menos poderosos del mundo tras la pandemia, ordenados en un detallado gráfico La pregunta más difícil. En estos momentos, la investigación continúa precisamente porque todavía faltan piezas importantes para reconstruir esas tres décadas: cómo consiguió trabajar, qué documentación empleó durante esos años o qué mecanismos le permitieron desarrollar su vida diaria sin residencia legal. Plus: tampoco se había comunicado todavía una sentencia definitiva ni una decisión final sobre su posible deportación a Corea del Sur. Lo único cerrado en estos momentos es la extraordinaria cronología: Japón le permitió entrar durante dos semanas en septiembre de 1993 y no descubrió su prolongadísima estancia hasta el verano de 2026. noticias.titulo: Vanished Texas bird island is back, with 2,500 pairs of birds
noticias.resumen: After years of erosion and extreme weather, Dickinson Bay's lost islands have seen a remarkable revival. Spearheaded by the Galveston Bay Foundation and U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, habitat restoration efforts have successfully created new nesting habitats for over 2,500 pairs of waterbirds. This revitalization not only boosts local biodiversity but also creates job opportunities and enhances economic activity through recreational fishing and improved oyster reefs.

noticias.titulo: A “quantum bath” puts quantum entanglement on autopilot
noticias.resumen: Physicists have demonstrated a new way to entangle distant quantum bits without the constant measurements and active control normally required. The team created a “quantum bath,” a shared environment filled with correlated microwave photons that automatically pushes separated qubits into an entangled state and helps keep them there. The experiment confirms a theoretical prediction made more than 20 years ago and could offer a simpler way to connect modules in future quantum computers.

noticias.contenido: Dentro de poco hará dos años que Rafael Nadal Parera puso fin a su carrera profesional. Fue en noviembre de 2024, tras una Copa Davis que acabó truncando un colofón mejor. Cerraba un carrerón de varios récords, 22 títulos de Grand Slam y dos oros olímpicos. ¿Y qué hace ahora? En su familia hay para no aburrirse: academias deportivas, centros de salud, inversiones, hoteles, renovables, inmobiliario e incluso negocios relacionados con puertos para megayates. Y todo partiendo de un negocio pequeñito y sin apenas inversión. A sus 40 años , Rafa Nadal concedió una entrevista a CNBC desde Fuerteventura y lo recordaba así: "Mi padre fue un ejemplo muy positivo para mí en términos de dedicación y trabajo duro... fue capaz de construir la mayor empresa de cristales de Baleares empezando desde cero". Bonita historia que ahora, en una notaría de Manacor, se reconstruye. Y es mucho más interesante que el aburridísimo clásico “empezaron en un garaje”. La empresa . Vidres Mallorca nació alrededor de esa historia familiar. Se dedica al cristal plano y de todo tipo, además de persianas. Durante décadas estuvo controlada al 50% por Sebastián Nadal, padre de Rafa, y Toni Nadal, su hermano y antiguo entrenador del tenista durante 27 años. La propia empresa sitúa sus orígenes en 1982, aunque el Registro Mercantil fija la constitución de la sociedad en 1989 . Cuenta con tres plantas en Mallorca y sus instalaciones suman casi 5.000 metros cuadrados . Durante años fue el negocio familiar que permitió construir una buena parte de la base patrimonial de los Nadal. Fabrican para empresas como Climalit y concentran su actividad en Mallorca. Pero en 2026 ocurrió algo importante: después de 37 años de sociedad conjunta, Vidres Mallorca dejó de existir como estructura única. Los números . En su último ejercicio disponible antes de la escisión, Vidres Mallorca facturó 13,55 millones de euros y ganó 2,17 millones. Sus activos ascendían a 35,1 millones, frente a los 26,91 millones que declaraba en 2021. Entre sus propiedades había locales y viviendas repartidas por Son Servera, Manacor, Palma, Calvià y Sant Llorenç des Cardassar. Pero el negocio no se limita a sobrevivir. En 2025, el Govern balear declaró el proyecto de Vidres Mallorca como proyecto industrial estratégico: la compañía va a por una nueva planta con la que sustituir sus instalaciones actuales, modernizar maquinaria y aumentar su capacidad productiva. La escisión . El 18 de marzo de 2026, la junta general aprobó partir Vidres Mallorca en dos sociedades: Vidres Mallorca SXXI, que se queda con el negocio del cristal, y Rector Rubi Invest, que concentra el patrimonio inmobiliario. El reparto tampoco fue proporcional al antiguo 50/50: Sebastián Nadal se quedó con el 100% de una sociedad y Toni Nadal con el 100% de la otra. Ni la familia ni el Registro Mercantil explican públicamente el motivo de la operación. Solo consta que fue "debidamente consentido por los socios". El resultado, sin embargo, es cristalino: el negocio industrial y el ladrillo toman caminos separados después de casi cuatro décadas. “Vete con tu Kia” . Rafa paseando ante un concesionario, enamorándose de un Aston Martin y su padre cortando la fantasía de raíz: “¿Qué vas a hacer con un Aston Martin en Manacor? Venga, vete con el Kia ”. Nada de delirios de grandeza: mientras Rafa acumulaba trofeos, Sebastián se encargaba de que los millones no se evaporaran. Sebastián Nadal ha sido la figura clave en la gestión financiera de su hijo. Administra, entre otras estructuras, la SICAV Growth Inversiones, y ha participado durante años en la organización patrimonial que rodea al tenista. La familia ha ido construyendo así un entramado empresarial que hoy tiene poco que ver con aquella fábrica de vidrio de Manacor. Más allá de las ventanas del padre . Rafa gestiona buena parte de sus negocios a través de Aspemir, el holding familiar administrado por su madre, Ana María Parera. La sociedad cerró 2024 con 375,4 millones de euros de patrimonio neto , además de 41,9 millones de ingresos y 14,5 millones de beneficio. Aspemir controla más de una veintena de sociedades y participaciones. Ahí están la Rafa Nadal Academy de Manacor, la cadena hotelera ZEL, desarrollada junto a Meliá (Mallorca, Costa Brava, Punta Cana y ahora Argentina ), y proyectos de nutrición y bienestar como NDL Pro-Health, creado junto a Cantabria Labs. También hay inversiones inmobiliarias, energías renovables, participaciones financieras y la productora Komodo, vinculada a proyectos como Mad Cool y producciones audiovisuales para Netflix. El grupo sigue creciendo . En 2026, Nadal ha reforzado la expansión internacional de su academia mediante International Tennis Academies, una estructura concebida para llevar el modelo de la Rafa Nadal Academy a otros mercados. Además, ha entrado en un negocio bastante menos obvio para un tenista: las marinas para grandes embarcaciones. Aspemir tomó una participación minoritaria en Ocean Platform Marinas, compañía dedicada al desarrollo y gestión de puertos deportivos para megayates. Otra ruptura . Con los restaurantes Tatel y Totó pasó algo parecido a lo de Vidres Mallorca, aunque por motivos y protagonistas diferentes. En 2024, Nadal y Abel Matutes rompieron su alianza con Manuel Campos dentro de Mabel Hospitaliy. Nadal y Matutes conservaron la parte inmobiliaria y otras inversiones, mientras Campos pasó a controlar la rama de restauración. Del tenis al ladrillo de lujo . La otra gran pieza inmobiliaria está en Palya Invest, la sociedad que nació tras la ruptura de Mabel Capital. Rafa Nadal y Abel Matutes se quedaron con la parte inmobiliaria y otras inversiones, mientras que su antiguo socio Manuel Campos conservó el negocio de restauración de Tatel y Totó , el cual también tiene socios de la talla de Cristiano Ronaldo, Pau Gasol o Rudy Fernández. Palya tiene ahora entre manos un proyecto de más de 200 millones de euros en la Costa del Sol, junto a Sierra Blanca, para desarrollar cerca de un centenar de viviendas de lujo entre Estepona y Marbella. El proyecto incluye, además del turismo náutico, residencias en primera línea de playa y otra promoción en Nagüeles. El título . Desde junio de 2025, Rafael Nadal es formalmente marqués de Llevant de Mallorca , un título nobiliario hereditario concedido por Felipe VI. noticias.titulo: Todo lo que hay que saber para orientarse en el mundo de Hobonichi Techo 2027: la agendas japonesas que están conquistando todo el mundo
noticias.resumen: En 2001, los redactores de la web japonesa 'Hobo Nikkan Itoi Shinbun' se reunieron para hacer un brainstorming. noticias.contenido: En 2001, los redactores de la web japonesa 'Hobo Nikkan Itoi Shinbun' se reunieron para hacer un brainstorming. Buscaban ideas para crear productos de su marca, una especie de merchandising. Ahí fue donde alguien levantó la mano y dijo: " ¿y si hacemos una agenda? ". Nadie tenía ni idea de papelería, ni en el diseño de planificadores. Por eso, decidieron cortar por lo sano y hacer la agenda que ellos querrían usar. Encargaron 12.000 unidades y cruzaron los dedos. 25 años después, Hononichi factura más de 46 millones de euros , cotiza en Bolsa y depende casi enteramente (un 67,4%) de esa agenda. Es, sin exagerar ni una milésima, un fenómeno global que tiene a decenas de miles de personas pendientes de una sola fecha: el 1 de septiembre a las 04:00 (horario de la península). El momento en que empieza la venta de 2027. Aquí os explicamos todo lo que hay que saber. En Xataka En la era digital, Japón ha convertido las agendas de papel en un fenómeno de masas gracias a una palabra: Hobonichi ¿Qué es Hobonichi Techo? Como acabo de explicar, se trata de una agenda. En su formato original, un tomo tamaño A6 (105 × 148 mm) de 195 gramos, capaz de abrirse completamente plano y articulado bajo el principio de "una página por día" (con una cuadrícula gris muy sutil impresa y un papel - el Tomoe River - mítico por su calidad). Con el paso de los años, Hobonichi ha pasado a ofrecer ocho formatos distintos siguiendo más o menos las mismas ideas básicas. Además de eso, la empresa lanza cada año toda una serie de 'complementos' (sobre todo, 'fundas' protectoras) que suelen agotar sus tiradas. Y muchas de ellas nunca más se vuelven a producir. Pero, antes de avanzar, hablemos del papel. Porque muy en el fondo la fama de las hobonichi viene de ahí. El Tomoe River es un papel ultrafino (de 52gr.) que aguanta todo tipo de tintas (desde estilográficas a acuarela) sin traspasar. Es lo que permite meter 365 días en un tomo de ese tamaño sin morir en el intento. Es verdad que hace unos pocos años tuvieron que cambiar de fabricante , pero a grandes rasgos el papel sigue ahí. Es la pieza clave que hace que la agenda sirva para planificar, sí; pero también para hacer journaling o directamente para pintar sin tener más cuidado del necesario. Los formatos de Hobonichi Hagamos un pequeño repaso: la Original es la más conocida, la básica y la que suele verse más. la Cousin es su 'hermana mayor'. Mucha gente que hace journaling la prefiere porque da más espacio. la Weeks es la opción más sencilla para usar como agenda (y llevar algunos 'habits trackers') las Avec facilitan la vida a mucha gente porque permiten usar el sistema con un grosor más manejable (sobre todo si haces journaling, scrapbooking o collage) la HON (que significa 'libro' en japonés) es para todos aquellos que no quieren comprar una funda. Las cousin y las original tienen unas cubiertas relativamente frágiles. Están pensadas para ir dentro de algo que las proteja. Las HON son autónomas. Formato ¿Cómo es? Tamaño Grosos/Peso idioma original Vista de año + Vista de mes 1 página 1 día A6 15 mm / ~195 g JP/EN cousin Vista de año + Vista de mes 1 página 1 día + semana vista A5 18 mm / ~445 g JP/EN weeks Vista de año + Vista de mes Semana vista + Hoja de notas Con tapa Cartera 11 mm / ~133 g JP/EN avec Igual que la original o la cousin, pero Dos tomos semestrales A6 o A5 8 mm / ~110 g cada uno 10 mm / ~260 g cada uno JP hon Igual que la original o la cousin, pero Con tapa dira integrada A6 o A5 16 mm / 20 mm JP/EN day-free Mensual + Páginas cuadriculadas sin fechar A6 o A5 JP planner 1 página 1 día. Solo en inglés A6 15 mm / ~190 g EN cinco años Cinco años en la misma página A6 o A5 25 mm JP Algunas claves prácticas: Empieza la semana en lunes en todas las ediciones salvo la Original japonesa, (que ofrece inicio en domingo o en lunes). La Original, la Cousin y la week s tienen además edición de abril (abril 2027 – marzo 2028), solo en japonés. Sale a la venta el 1 de febrero de 2027 a las 11:00 JST. La day-free cubre de 16 meses. La de cinco años cubre de 2027 a 2031. Llevan funda aparte: Original, Avec, Planner, Cousin, day-free. Van con tapa propia: HON, weeks y cinco años. Aunque las weeks también tienen fundas opcionales a parte. Las fundas de A6 Original valen también para la day-free A6; las de A5 Cousin, para la day-free A5. Vayamos a los diseños Lo cierto es que las agendas en sí no suelen agotarse. Lo que se agotan son las ediciones especiales. Cada año, Hobonichi se asocia con numerosos creadores de contenidos, marcas o IP, para producir todo tipo de accesorios con los que acompañar a la agenda. Por eso el revuelo: durante todo agosto, la marca japonesa ha ido mostrando sus nuevos diseños y la red se ha llenado de análisis y comentarios . Y, ojo, aquí hay que andarse con cuidado porque no todo está disponible fuera de Japón. De hecho, hay cosas que solo se venderán en tiendas concretas. El catálogo cada año es casi infinito (y muy caro); pero aquí os dejamos una pequeña selección de los diseños que más circulan en redes. 'Colors': Colección de colores lisos Colaboración con 'beautiful people', una marca de ropa diseñada por Hidenori Kumakiri Unas conocidas marionetas japonesas Colaboración con la diseñadora y directora de arte japonesa Yoshie Watanabe Colaboración con la marca Natal Desing Colaboración con el Victoria & Albert Museum de Londres Colaboración con Yumi Kitagishi Colaboración con la prestigiosa marca de moda y diseño japonesa fundada en 1995 por el diseñador Akira Minagawa ¿Cómo se compra? Hay dos opciones fundamentales: o en la web oficial o en las papelerías asociadas. En España y en Latino América hay varias de ellas. La web oficial tiene productos únicos y lo envía a muchos países. noticias.titulo: En 2009, 23 bisontes llegaron a México metidos en un camión. Hoy ya son más de 500: la historia de conservación más ambiciosa del desierto norteamericano
noticias.resumen: En 2009, veintitrés bisontes salieron del Wind Cave National Park, en Dakota del Sur, con destino al norte de Chihuahua. Los bisontes nunca habían desaparecido de México , pero les faltaba poco. Apenas quedaba un hatillo silvestre que cruzaba la frontera con Nuevo México de vez en cuando. Diecisiete años después, la Reserva de la Biosfera de Janos ya no tiene 23 ejemplares, sino más de 460. México en su conjunto, acumula más 600 repartidos en tres poblaciones (con una cuarta ya en marcha). En resumen: no es una historia más. Es la historia de conservación más ambiciosa del desierto…
noticias.contenido: En 2009, veintitrés bisontes salieron del Wind Cave National Park, en Dakota del Sur, con destino al norte de Chihuahua. Los bisontes nunca habían desaparecido de México , pero les faltaba poco. Apenas quedaba un hatillo silvestre que cruzaba la frontera con Nuevo México de vez en cuando. Diecisiete años después, la Reserva de la Biosfera de Janos ya no tiene 23 ejemplares, sino más de 460. México en su conjunto, acumula más 600 repartidos en tres poblaciones (con una cuarta ya en marcha). En resumen: no es una historia más. Es la historia de conservación más ambiciosa del desierto norteamericano. El desierto recuperándose a sí mismo. Cuando el 27 de noviembre de 2025 se liberaron 44 bisontes (38 hembras y 6 machos) en la Reserva El Santuario, a pocos kilómetros de Cuatro Ciénegas de Carranza, nadie se imaginaba que solo harían falta nueve meses para que rebrotaran los pastos, volvieran los escarabajos peloteros, detectáramos pumas, linces y pecaríes en las cámaras trampa o que nacieran ocho crías de bisonte. Esa "es" la noticia: el desierto está recuperándose rapidísimamente. De hecho, según los investigadores, " teníamos monitoreando cinco años ese espacio y el día uno que llegó el bisonte, apareció inmediatamente el puma". No es magia, es pura conservación; pero sobre el papel... se parece mucho. En Xataka La reintroducción del lobo y el oso ha provocado un sinfín de problemas en la España vaciada. Ahora le toca el turno al bisonte europeo Tanto que merece la pena ser prudentes. Sabemos (y muy bien) que un megaherbívoro transforma el pastizal del sitio en el que vive. En el Konza Prairie de Kansas lo llevan estudiando más de treinta años : reintroducir el bisonte provoca que la diversidad de plantas nativas se duplique y, ojo, supuso la mejor defensa para una de las peores sequías que se recuerdan en las Grandes Llanuras. Pero esa es también la trampa: si algo hemos aprendido de Kansas es que los ecosistemas tardan en encajar de nuevo. Los pastos altos de Konza Prairie no tienen nada que ver con el matorral xerófilo de Chihuahua. Nadie sabe qué va a pasar y celebrar los primeros nueve meses está bien, pero es precipitado. El gran problema. No obstante, el problema es otro. No hemos empezado este artículo por los 23 bisontes de Wind Cave por casualidad: un equipo encabezado por Domínguez-Viveros genotipó 174 animales y se dio cuenta de que la población es demasiado parecida a nivel genético. Todo el edificio de la reintroducción del bisonte viene de esos 23 y si no se toman medidas, los problemas de consanguinidad aumentan a razón de un 4% con cada generación. Es más, la IUNC la sigue catalogando como especie 'casi amenazada': en cualquier momento, puede tener serios problemas. Y, más allá de eso, hay muchos más problemas. El caso de Cuatro Ciénegas es un caso paradigmático de que el bisonte es lo de menos: no hablamos de un pastizal, sino de un sistema de manantiales y pozas que, desde 1987, lleva siendo sangrado por los agricultores locales ( y está a punto del colapso ). La laguna de Churince se secó por completo hace no demasiado. No es que la zona no sea ecológicamente importante. Solo en especies endémicas se cuentan: 23 taxones vegetales, 9 peces, 10 moluscos y 6 crustáceos. Peor nada de eso es realmente llamativo. Ahí es donde, curiosamente, entra el bisonte. La historia nunca ha sido que un megaherbívoro ha reparado el desierto. Sino que, un megaherbívoro puede actuar como escudo simbólico de un ecosistema valiosísimo que no dejamos de hostigar. A menudo, criticamos la idea de que las especies 'estrella' (porque se llevan toda la atención). Pero este es un uso muy creativo de todo esto porque si triunfa la imagen icónica del bisonte, la presión por conservar Cuatro Ciénegas será mucho más alta. Y eso sí que sí, será una buena noticia. Imagen | Yohan Marion En Xataka | Todos los expertos coinciden en que introducir los bisonte en España es una mala idea. Y, aún así, lo estamos haciendo - La noticia En 2009, 23 bisontes llegaron a México metidos en un camión. Hoy ya son más de 500: la historia de conservación más ambiciosa del desierto norteamericano fue publicada originalmente en Xataka por Javier Jiménez .
